A stamp is more real than a fact.

The letter from the province arrived on a Tuesday in a brown envelope with a window in it and sat on the desk for four hours before anybody opened it, because everybody in that building knew what a brown envelope with a window is.

It asked for three things. The complete register of consultations and disposals for eleven months. The practising certificate of the signing physician. And a date, in Dey, on which an officer would attend.
Nasrin read it twice and put it down and said, "Well."

And then she did something I did not expect, which was to laugh — one syllable, out of the nose, entirely without pleasure — and say, "Eleven months. Four hundred and eleven signatures. Three hundred and something referrals. And they have written to me because a woman did not die."
I want to say what I understood in that room, because it is the only thing I know that is worth anything and it took me forty-six years and four professions to arrive at it.
*The state of this country is not looking for the truth. It has never been looking for the truth. It is looking for a document that is consistent with itself.*

I know this the way a plumber knows about water. I have spent my adult life going in and out of a system that is supposed to catch me, and it has caught me once, and it caught me because an eighty-four-year-old woman fell over, not because of anything anybody wrote down.

Consider what had actually gone unnoticed. A doctor with an eleven-year record had stopped practising and nobody in any office anywhere had registered it, because the returns kept coming and the returns were correct. A nurse had signed a physician's name four hundred and eleven times and no human being had ever compared two of those signatures, because there was no reason to and no mechanism for it and nobody whose job it was. A burglar had walked into a health post off a bus and practised medicine for fourteen weeks on a laminated card he found in a bag, and the province had sent him three circulars, a vaccination schedule and a form about hepatitis.
None of that produced a letter.
What produced a letter was a form that was right, at three in the morning, in a place where nobody expects right.

That is not corruption. I want to be careful, because it would be much more comfortable if it were corruption. Nobody in that provincial office was crooked. They were doing exactly the job as described: matching numbers to numbers. A system that matches numbers to numbers will catch every inconsistency and no lies whatsoever, and it is the same in every ministry in every country and ours has simply had longer to perfect it.
I had spent my whole life on the wrong side of the paperwork, going through windows.
It took me until that Tuesday to notice that the window had never been the way in.

Eleven months in one night.
I did it on the Thursday, alone, from eight in the evening to about five in the morning, with the generator going and the door locked.

Nasrin knew I was going to do it and did not stay. That was not cowardice. That was her being extremely intelligent, because a person who was not in the room can say she was not in the room and that is the only asset either of us had left.
Here is what I did, and I am going to set it out properly, because it is the most skilled work of my life and it is a crime and both of those are true.

The register had eleven months of entries in one hand — hers. Four hundred and eleven signatures in a second hand, forged — also hers, and honestly not very well; she is a nurse, not a burglar, and a forgery made four hundred times by a tired woman at the end of a shift drifts, and hers had drifted about two millimetres to the right over eleven months in a way that any competent examiner would find in an afternoon.
I could not undo that. Nobody could undo that.
So I did the other thing.
I did not remove the forgery. *I explained it.*

I wrote a new document. Twenty-two pages, in my own hand, dated across eleven months in eleven different inks, using four pens I had been buying one at a time in Sabzevar for three weeks. It was a supervision log — the kind of thing a supervising physician keeps on a nurse practising under delegated authority in a remote post, which is a real category, which exists in the regulations, which Behnam had a copy of on the shelf in the back room and which I got Nasrin to read to me twice without telling her why.

In the new document, Dr Behnam Ardalani was unwell from Farvardin. He was under treatment. He remained in the post, in residence, exercising clinical oversight, and had — with a written delegation, which I also wrote, and which took me two hours to get right — authorised his nurse to record and dispose under his authority, countersigning in batches, which accounts for the drift, because a man signing forty at a time signs the fortieth differently from the first.
Every decision she made became a decision he supervised.
Every signature she forged became a signature he delegated.

And every single thing that could not be made to fit either of those — nine referrals, two disposals, a controlled drug entry from Aban that I could not account for by any route — I moved onto myself.
Onto the locum. Onto the man on the laminated card. Onto a name off a bus luggage rack.
Which is the part I want to put down plainly.

I have wondered about him for twenty years. He was born eleven months before me. He was on a bus in Sabzevar in the autumn and he put a bag on a rack over row eleven and got off somewhere and it was not there. He reported it or he did not. He got another card or he did not.

And in a file in a provincial health office there is now a locum who attended Ab-Bidar for fourteen weeks, made nine decisions of questionable judgement, and left without notice, and that file has his number on it.
I do not know what it cost him. It may have cost him nothing. It may have cost him a great deal.

I sat at that desk for nine hours and made a woman innocent and a sick man dignified and a stranger culpable, and I did it well, and at about four in the morning I understood that I had finally found the thing I was actually good at, and that it had taken until forty-six, and that there was no version of the world in which I could ever do it again for anybody who would know my name.

I would like to tell you that this was conscience.

It was not conscience. I want to be accurate. I sat there and I thought about the father, who cannot read, and about the uncle, who can, and about the fact that a village of four hundred people already knows exactly what happened and does not need a document to know it — and I understood that changing that card would not deceive one single person who mattered. It would only deceive the province.
And I did not want to be a man who had lied to the province about that particular thing. Not because it would be wrong. Because it would be *cheap*.

I took the shoes, which were oiled now, twice, left overnight, and which were still half a size too big and always will be.

At the top of the village I stopped at the shop, which is also the bus stop and also where the mail goes, and the man on the pallets was not there because it was half past four in the morning, and I sat on the pallets and waited for the six o'clock and looked back down at four hundred people in the dark.
The generator was running.

Three men.

Yadollah told it to me wrong. I know that now — I have since had it told to me properly by somebody who had read it, and there were seven valleys and not seven deserts, and there were far more birds than he remembered, and every one of them stood up and gave an excuse.
But he had the two that mattered, and I have thought about the wrong one for twenty years.

I thought the nightingale was a fool. I said so out loud in a clinic in front of a man who had gone down the same hole four hundred and eleven times, a woman who had not left a building in eleven months, and a doctor in a back room, and every one of them had stayed for a rose of one kind or another and I was the only person present who had not.
And Yadollah said the rose only lasts a week and the bird knows that and stays anyway.
I have got on eleven buses in my life at half past four in the morning.

Here is what I could not have understood at the time and can only just about hold now. The nightingale is not the sad one in that poem. The nightingale has something. He is standing in a garden, in front of everybody, saying this, here, is worth more than the journey — and he is wrong, and he knows he is wrong, and he stays.
The one who has nothing is the one who goes.
I have been three men and every one of them left, and I have started to suspect that I am not the traveller in this story. I think I might be the road.

I was standing at the side of a road outside a town I do not intend to name, waiting for a lift, at about four in the afternoon.
She said, "Is that Sayyid Vahedi?"

I said, "It is."

I said that was good.

"So." A pause. "There's a thing. In Bahman. It's not a wedding, it's after the wedding, my husband's family do a thing, and my mother's coming, and there's a — look, it's stupid, I've been trying to work out how to say this for two days."
I did not say anything.

"You're the only person," she said, "who ever gave me an answer about him that I could actually use. Everybody else wanted me to arrive somewhere. You said I was allowed. And I wrote it down and I've still got it on my phone and I have read it, honestly, probably a hundred times."

"I'd like you to come," she said. "If you can. I know it's a long way and I know you must get asked all the time. But I'd like there to be one person there who knows the whole of it."
One person there who knows the whole of it.

I stood at the side of a road in a dead man's shoes, oiled twice and left overnight, and was invited to my daughter's celebration by my daughter, in the character of the priest I invented in order to avoid being her father, on the grounds that I am the only person alive who knows the truth about her.
Which is correct.
I said I would try to come.
She said, "Really?"
And I said, "Really."

And she made a small noise — one syllable, out of the nose, entirely with pleasure, and I had heard it before, on the other side of a desk in a shrine office, when she was doing nine minutes about me and I laughed at the good bit.

I have not put the telephone down yet. That is not a figure of speech; I am telling you where I am. Everything you have read from the first page was written in the ninety days between that afternoon and Bahman, and I wrote it because I did not know what else to do with my hands, and because you are going to have to know all of it before you can understand what I did next.
Somebody is going to have to be standing in that room in Bahman.
I have been three men.
I do not yet know how many I will need.
